# Comparative study of the physicochemical properties, volatile compounds, and bacterial microbiota in commercial and traditional yak yogurt from the Qinghai–Tibet plateau

**Authors:** Juan Song; Yiheng Li; Longlin Wang; Jinliang Zhang; Chengrui Shi; Liwen Zhong; Caihong Liu; Mailin Song; Xinyun Yu; Weibing Zhang; Pengcheng Wen

**Affiliations:** aCollege of Food Science and Engineering, Gansu Agricultural University, Lanzhou 730070, China | bAgricultural Product Storage and Processing Research Institute, Gansu Academy of Agricultural Sciences, Lanzhou 730070, China

## Abstract

This study aimed to elucidate differences between the commercial starter culture (CK) and traditional starters from different Tibetan regions (Gannan (GN), Qinghai (QH), Tibet (XZ)) in fermenting yak yogurt by physicochemical properties, flavor, and bacterial community. Results indicated acidity, proline, arginine, alanine, and C6:0 contents were significantly higher in the traditional starter culture than CK (P < 0.05). Gas chromatography-ion mobility spectrometry analysis found the traditional starter culture group was dominated by alcohols and esters, whereas CK exhibited richer ketones. Metagenomic analysis revealed Lactobacillus delbrueckii (49.56% in XZ, 24.86% in GN) and Streptococcus spp. (18.30% in CK, 17.21% in QH) as the dominant. Moreover, pH and titratable acidity were primary factors affecting microbial diversity. Meanwhile, glutamic acid modulated ester biosynthesis like ethyl acetate, while C16:0 fatty acids inhibited off-odor ketones such as 2-pentanone. This study offers valuable insights into developing specialized fermentation agents and standardizing the quality of yak yogurt.

Keywords: Yak yogurt, Traditional fermentation starter, HS–GC–IMS, Metagenomics, Bacterial community

## Abstract

## Abstract

Traditionally fermented yak yogurt had higher acidity and amino acid content.

Traditional fermented yak yogurt contains higher levels of alcohols and esters.

Commercially fermented yak yogurt was richer in ketones.

Lactobacillus delbrueckii and Streptococcus spp. were the dominant in yak yogurt.

pH and total acidity influenced the microbial diversity of yak yogurt.

## Introduction

The yak (Bos grunniens) is a cold-adapted livestock species found on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. Yak-derived products are rich in high-quality protein, essential amino acids, and unsaturated fats, rendering them as important components of Tibetan cuisine (Li, Guo, Yang, et al., 2024; Shah et al., 2023). Yak yogurt is an integral part of nomadic diets. It contains a variety of microbes, primarily lactic acid bacteria (e.g., Lactobacillus spp.), introduced through traditional starters locally known as “Yinzi,” which are remnants of previously fermented yak yogurt batches. The complex secondary metabolites in yak yogurt contribute to its distinct regional flavor and probiotic properties, distinguishing it from yogurt that is commercially produced using standard starters (Kondrotiene, Zavistanaviciute, Aksomaitiene, Novoslavskij and Malakauskas, 2023a, Kondrotiene, Zavistanaviciute, Aksomaitiene, Novoslavskij and Malakauskas, 2023b; Zhang et al., 2022). The acidity and flavor of yogurt produced from traditional starters vary according to environmental factors, including regional differences in microbial composition; this diminishes the consistency of industrially produced yogurt (Zhang et al., 2022; Zinno et al., 2022). Meanwhile, commercial starters guarantee more predictable acidity, but their simplified microbial composition compromises the nutritional and flavor complexity of yak yogurt (Bintsis & Papademas, 2022). This indicates that commercial and traditional starters employ distinct regulatory mechanisms during yogurt fermentation.

Studies have shown that the flavor of yak yogurt relies heavily on the microbial metabolic network. Lactic acid bacteria synthesize key flavor compounds through multiple metabolic pathways: glycolysis produces lactic acid, proteolysis releases free amino acids, and lipolysis generates short-chain fatty acids. These metabolites interact to form alcohols and esters that contribute to the final flavor profile (Liu et al., 2020). Tibetan yak yogurt has a tropical fruity aroma because of the phenylethanol generated by Lactobacillus spp. through phenylalanine metabolism (Peng et al., 2021a, Peng et al., 2021b). Qinghai yak yogurt has elevated ester levels owing to the high esterase activity of Lactococcus spp. (Ding, Mi, Zhou, Ke and Guo, 2022a, Ding, Mi, Zhou, Ke and Guo, 2022b).

Metagenomics enables the study and detailed mapping of microbe–metabolite interactions by using gene annotation methods such as Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis (Zhang et al., 2025a, Zhang et al., 2025b). Using metagenomics, a study showed that Lactobacillus helveticus uses the tyrDC gene to control aromatic compound production in Mongolian fermented mare's yogurt (Su et al., 2025). Two main gaps exist in our understanding of how commercial and traditional starters affect yak yogurt quality on the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau. The impact of microbial specificity in different regions, such as Gannan, Qinghai, and Tibet, on the properties and flavor of yak yogurt is not well understood. Additionally, no study has systematically investigated the effects of standardizing the production of commercial starters on the nutritional profile of yak yogurt, as well as the links between metabolites and key microbes in traditional starters. To address these gaps, this study conducted a systematic comparison of traditional starters from three major ecological zones: Gannan (eastern fringe, lower altitude, agro-pastoral), Qinghai (central-northeastern, medium nomadic), and Tibet (southwestern core, high-altitude nomadic). We aimed to test the hypotheses that starters from these distinct environments harbor unique microbial consortia, and these differences confer distinct physicochemical and sensory properties to the final yogurt, differentiating them from products made with commercial starters.

This study investigated the properties of yak yogurt fermented using commercial starter cultures (CK) and traditional indigenous starter cultures from Gannan (GN), Qinghai (QH), and Tibet (XZ). The influence of starter culture origin on yogurt quality was assessed through physicochemical analyses, flavor compound identification, and metagenomic sequencing. This study establishes a theoretical framework for region-specific starter culture development.

## Materials and methods

### Chemicals and reagents

YO-MIX 883 commercial starter culture, containing a blend of L. delbrueckii spp. and Streptococcus thermophilus, was provided by Danisco Biotechnology Co., Ltd. (Shanghai, China). Fresh yak yogurt was sourced from Liaoyuan Dairy Co., Ltd. (Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture). Amino acid standards and fatty acid methyl ester standards (purity ≥98%) were purchased from WAKO. Acetonitrile, methanol, n-hexane, phenyl isothiocyanate, 2-methyl-3-heptanone, and L-leucine (purity ≥99.9%) were obtained from OCEANPAK. MRS medium, hydrochloric acid, sodium chloride, phenolphthalein, sodium hydroxide, and 2-butanone were purchased from Sinopharm Chemical Reagent Co., Ltd.

### Collection and activation of yak yogurt starter cultures

Traditional yak yogurt fermentation agents (i.e. microbial inoculants retained by households, rather than finished yogurt) were collected in May 2022 from low, medium, and high-altitude pastoral areas on the Qinghai Tibet Plateau where yaks were concentrated. All samples were obtained directly from local herder families according to the long-standing family fermentation method. Twenty-one samples collected from the Gannan Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture (Xiaba Gou, Tawa Village, and Bola Village) were combined to create a composite sample, which was subsequently randomized into three experimental groups, labeled as GN1, GN2, and GN3; Fifteen samples collected from the Qinghai Tibetan Autonomous Prefecture (Xiuma Township, Zhihema Township, and Zhihelang Village) were combined to create a composite sample, which was subsequently randomized into three experimental groups, labeled as QH1, QH2, and QH3; Eighteen samples collected from the Xizang Autonomous Region (Zepu Village, Laguo Village and Gongda Village) were combined to create a composite sample, which was subsequently randomized into three experimental groups, labeled as XZ1, XZ2 and XZ3. The basic information of the sampling points can be found in supplementary material Table S1. Sampling is carried out by professionally trained personnel to ensure consistency and standardized operation of sampling methods. Each serving contains approximately 50 mL of fermentation agents . Take 5 mL and transfer it to a sterile enzyme free freezer tube (Corning, USA). The aliquots were flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, transported to the laboratory within 24 h, and stored at −80 °C until analysis.

Under sterile conditions, 0.06 g each of both traditional and commercial starter cultures were rehydrated in 100 mL of physiological saline for 30 min and subsequently inoculated (using two separate loops) into MRS broth medium. The cultures were incubated under anaerobic conditions at 37 °C for 24 h in a YQX-II anaerobic incubator (Yuejin Medical Instrument, Shanghai, China). This cycle was repeated for three consecutive passages. Subsequently, subculturing was carried out with an inoculum volume of 3% using logarithmic phase bacterial. Determine the viable cell concentration (CFU/mL) using the dilution plate counting method(Garre et al., 2019). Perform a tenfold serial dilution (from 10−1 to 10−8) of the logarithmic phase bacterial solution with sterile saline. Spread 100 μL of each dilution evenly onto MRS agar plates, with three replicates for each dilution level. Incubate the plates statically at 37 °C in a constant temperature incubator (Thermo, USA) for 48 h before counting. Select colony counts ranging between 30 and 300 for statistical analysis. The viable cell count of Lactobacillus spp. was determined by standard plate counting on MRS agar and was consistently maintained at 5.00 × 107 CFU/mL, thus obtaining a standardized yak yogurt fermentation starter suitable for subsequent fermentation experiments.

### Preparation of yak yogurt

Yak yogurt was prepared following a traditional method used by Tibetan pastoralists (Li, Yang, Tang, et al., 2024). Fresh yak milk was boiled and allowed to cool naturally to approximately 50 °C. Then, 5% (w/w) traditional or commercial starter culture was added to the yak milk. The mixture was placed in a pinewood barrel wrapped in wool felt to maintain warmth and fermented for 5–6 h, allowing the yogurt to coagulate, the viable counts in the final yogurts reached a final concentration of (8.90 ± 0.3) × 108 CFU/mL. Yak yogurt was collected in 50 mL sterile tubes and immediately frozen for later analysis.

### pH determination

The pH was determined using a previously described method with slight modifications (Matela et al., 2019). 1.0 g of sample was homogenized with 10 mL of sterile distilled water and centrifuged at 8000 ×g for 10 min at 4 °C in the Centrifuge 5804 R instrument (Eppendorf, Germany). The pH of the supernatant was measured using the PB-10 pH meter (Sartorius AG, Germany), which was calibrated with standard buffer solutions at pH 4.01, 7.00, and 9.21.

### Total acidity determination

The total acidity was determined using a previously described method with slight modifications (Moonga et al., 2021). 0.5 mL of the supernatant sample (see Section 2.3) was diluted with 9.5 mL of ultrapure water, and 10 μL of 1% phenolphthalein indicator was added. The solution was titrated with 0.01 M sodium hydroxide until a persistent faint pink endpoint was observed. The total acidity, expressed as lactic acid concentration, was calculated using the following titration formula:

$$ Total Acidity g / L = V NaOH × C NaOH × 90 V sample $$

where VNaOH denotes volume of sodium hydroxide titrant used (mL); CNaOH denotes concentration of sodium hydroxide solution (0.01 mol/L); Vsample denotes sample volume (0.5 mL); and 90 is the molar mass conversion factor for lactate.

### Amino acid quantification

The amino acid content was quantified using a previously described method with slight modifications (Ulmer et al., 2022). The homogenate was collected from the central layer and centrifuged at 12,000 ×g for 15 min at 4 °C in the Centrifuge 5804 R instrument (Eppendorf, Germany). The resulting supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 μm membrane filter. A 200 μL aliquot of the filtered supernatant was spiked with 20 μL of norleucine internal standard (10 μg/mL), followed by the sequential addition of 100 μL of triethylamine/acetonitrile (1:1 v/v) and 100 μL of phenylisothiocyanate/acetonitrile (1:100, v/v). The mixture was vortexed and incubated in the dark at 25 °C for 1 h. Post-derivatization, extraction was performed with 1 mL of n-hexane. The aqueous phase was diluted fivefold, filtered, and prepared for chromatographic analysis.

Chromatography was performed on the Agilent 1100 series high-performance liquid chromatography system (Agilent Technologies, USA), equipped with an Amethyst C18—H column (250 × 4.6 mm, 5 μm; Sepax Technologies). The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, with a flow rate set to 1 mL/min and an injection volume of 10 μL. To prepare mobile phase A, 7.6 g of anhydrous sodium acetate was dissolved in 925 mL of water. The pH was adjusted to 6.5 with glacial acetic acid. Finally, 70 mL of acetonitrile was added, and the buffer was filtered through a 0.45 μm membrane. Mobile phase B was an aqueous solution of 80% acetonitrile. The gradient elution program was as follows: 0–2 min, 0% mobile phase B; 2–15 min, linear increase of mobile phase B from 0% to 10%; 15–25 min, linear increase of mobile phase B from 10% to 30%; 25–33 min, linear increase of mobile phase B from 30% to 45%; 33–33.1 min, linear increase of mobile phase B from 45% to 100%; 33.1–38 min, isocratic at 100% mobile phase B; 38–38.1 min, linear decrease of mobile phase B from 100% to 0%; 38.1–45 min, re-equilibration at 0% mobile phase B. The precision of the instrument was assessed by six consecutive injections of a derivatized standard, yielding relative standard deviations (RSD) of 0.15% to 0.82% for all 17 amino acid peaks. Method repeatability, evaluated from six independently prepared sample replicates, showed RSD of 1.34% to 2.35% for amino acid content. The derivatized sample solution remained stable at room temperature for 24 h, with RSD for peak areas between 0.32% and 0.77%. Derivatization efficiency and accuracy were confirmed by standard addition experiments (n = 6), which gave mean recoveries of 95.83% to 100.04% for the target amino acids (all associated RSD < 3%) and a recovery of 92.5% (RSD < 5%) for the internal standard, norleucine. The limits of detection (LOD, S/N = 3) and quantification (LOQ, S/N = 10) for the amino acids were 0.05–0.21 μg/mL and 0.17–0.70 μg/mL, respectively. Quantification was performed using the internal standard method. The concentration of the target amino acid was calculated using the following formula:

$$ C μg / mL = F 1 F 2 × C standard $$

where F1 denotes chromatographic peak area of each amino acid in the sample solution normalized to the internal standard peak area; F2 denotes chromatographic peak area of each amino acid in the mixed amino acid standard solution normalized to the internal standard peak area; and Cs tan dard denotes concentration of the amino acid standard solution.

### Fatty acid profiling and quantification

Fatty acid profiling and quantification were performed using a previously described method with slight modifications (Paszczyk & Tońska, 2022). For sample preparation, fatty acid methyl esters (FAMEs) were prepared via acid-catalyzed esterification, 1 mL of the sample supernatant was combined with 2 mL of 2.5% (v/v) sulfuric acid-in-methanol reagent. To prevent oxidative degradation during the reaction, 0.1% (w/v) butylated hydroxytoluene (BHT) was added to the mixture. Heptadecanoic acid methyl ester (C17:0, Sigma-Aldrich) was used as an internal standard and was added to the sample prior to derivatization at a known concentration. The mixture was then incubated at 80 °C for 1 h and cooled. Recovery of the internal standard from six replicate spiked samples ranged from 94.10% to 101.60%, with a relative standard deviation (RSD) below 5%.Following derivatization, FAMEs were extracted thrice by adding 5 mL of n-hexane and 1 mL of saturated sodium chloride solution each time. The n-hexane extracts were pooled, concentrated under a nitrogen stream, and reconstituted to a final volume of 1 mL prior to filtration and subsequent chromatographic analysis.

Chromatography was performed on the Agilent 6890 N Network gas chromatograph (Agilent Technologies, USA) equipped with a WM-CN100 capillary column (100 m × 0.25 mm × 0.2 μm). The flame ionization detector was maintained at 260 °C. The temperature program spanned from 0 to 51 min, with a temperature ramp from 140 °C to 240 °C and a split injection ratio of 10:1.

For calibration curve generation, precisely weighed fatty acid methyl ester standards were dissolved in n-hexane to prepare 5–6 calibration solutions of varying concentrations. Each standard was analyzed sequentially under the specified chromatographic conditions to quantify the peak areas of individual fatty acid methyl esters. Calibration curves were obtained by plotting peak area (ordinate) against concentration (abscissa).

### Quantification of volatile flavor compounds

Volatile flavor compounds were quantified using a previously described method with slight modifications (Chi et al., 2024; A. Liu et al., 2022; van Hemert, 2018). 2.0 g of the sample was mixed with 20 μL of 20 ppm 2-methyl-3-heptanone internal standard in a headspace vial, followed by incubation at 60 °C for 15 min. The injection volume was set to 500 μL, and each sample was analyzed in triplicate.

The headspace sampling conditions were as follows: incubation temperature, 60 °C; incubation time, 15 min; injection volume, 500 μL; splitless injection; incubation speed, 500 r/min; syringe temperature, 85 °C.

Gas chromatography–ion mobility spectrometry (GC–IMS) was performed on the FlavourSpec® system (G.A.S., Dortmund, Germany) equipped with an MXT-5 column (15 m × 0.53 mm × 1.0 μm; Restek, USA) and a CTC-PAL 3 headspace autosampler (CTC Analytics AG, Zwingen, Switzerland). The column temperature was maintained at 60 °C, with high-purity nitrogen (purity ≥99.999%) as the carrier gas. The pressure program was as follows: initial flow rate of 2.0 mL/min held for 2 min, linearly increased to 10.0 mL/min over 8 min, and further increased to 100.0 mL/min over 10 min. The total chromatographic run time was 20 min, and the injection port temperature was maintained at 80 °C.

The ionization source was a tritium source (3H) operated in positive-ion mode, with a drift tube length of 53 mm, electric field strength of 500 V/cm, drift tube temperature of 45 °C, high-purity nitrogen (purity ≥99.999%) as the drift gas, and flow rate of 150 mL/min.

### Metagenomic detection and analysis

Metagenomic analysis was performed as previously described with modifications (Qu et al., 2024; Zhang, Lin, et al., 2025; Lou et al., 2023). 10 mL of yak yogurt was mixed with 90 mL of sterile phosphate-buffered saline (0.1 M, pH 7.4) and homogenized for 5 min in a sterile BagLight PolySilk bag. Microbial cells were pelleted by centrifugation (8000 ×g, 10 min, 4 °C). Total genomic DNA was extracted from the pellet using the DNeasy PowerFood Kit (Omega Bio-tek, USA). To monitor for contamination, an extraction reagent blank (containing all reagents but no sample) was processed in parallel with each batch. DNA quality was assessed by spectrophotometry (A260/A280: 1.8–2.0), agarose gel electrophoresis, and fluorometric quantification (Qubit 4.0, Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA).

Sequencing libraries were constructed from qualified DNA via ultrasonication, end-repair, A-tailing, adapter ligation, and PCR amplification. Library concentration and fragment size distribution were quantified using a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer and an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent, USA), respectively. Paired-end sequencing (2 × 150 bp) was performed on an Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform. Raw reads were processed with fastpto remove adapters and low-quality bases (Phred score < 20). Per sample, this yielded an average of 45–50 million high-quality reads (6.8–7.6 Gb), with Q30 > 95%, providing sufficient depth for downstream analysis.

Bioinformatic processing included host DNA removal by aligning quality-filtered reads to the yak reference genome (Bos grunniens) and discarding matches, typically reducing host-derived reads to <1%. Non-host reads from all samples were co-assembled using metaSPAdes (v3.15.0). Contigs were binned with MetaBAT2, MaxBin2, and CONCOCT, and consolidated with DAS Tool. Metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) were assessed with CheckM2, and those with >50% completeness and < 10% contamination were dereplicated at 95% average nucleotide identity using dRep. Functional gene annotation was performed on the predicted proteome from the non-redundant gene set. Open reading frames were predicted with Prodigal (v2.6.3), and the resulting amino acid sequences (length > 100 aa) were clustered using CD-HIT (v4.7; thresholds: ≥90% identity, ≥90% coverage) to generate a non-redundant gene catalog. Gene abundances were quantified by mapping quality-filtered reads from each sample back to this catalog using SOAPaligner (v2.21) with a 95% identity threshold. For KEGG annotation, the non-redundant amino acid sequences were aligned against the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) database (https://www.kegg.jp/) using BLASTP (v2.2.28+) with an E-value cutoff of ≤1 × 10−5. KEGG Orthology (KO) identifiers and their associated pathways were assigned based on the best hits. Differences in the abundance of KEGG pathways or KO terms between sample groups (e.g., traditional vs. commercial starters) were assessed using Student's t-tests (for pairwise comparisons), and overall functional profile dissimilarities were evaluated by permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA/Adonis) based on Bray-Curtis distances, implemented via the veganpackage in R. This shotgun metagenomics-based approach, employing direct sequence alignment rather than 16S rRNA gene-based prediction (e.g., PICRUSt2), ensures a more accurate representation of the community's functional potential. Predicted proteins were additionally annotated via eggNOG-mapper for KEGG/COG pathways, dbCAN3 for carbohydrate-active enzymes, and antiSMASH for biosynthetic gene clusters. Taxonomic classification was performed with GTDB-Tk (GTDB release 214). Contaminant sequences identified in the extraction blank were systematically subtracted from all sample datasets prior to analysis.

### Statistical analysis

All experimental results are expressed as mean ± standard deviation. Bioinformatics analysis was performed using the SPSS software, version 26.0 (SPSS Inc., Chicago, IL, USA), Origin 2022 software, and Genescloud software (https://www.genescloud.cn/chart/ChartOverview). Compounds were identified using the Laboratory Analytical Viewer software and the GC–IMS Library Search tool (built-in National Institute of Standards and Technology 2014 database and IMS database), both of which are built into the GC–IMS instrument. The “Reporter” plug-in in Laboratory Analytical Viewer was used to compare the GC–IMS spectra of samples, and the “Gallery Plot” plug-in was used to compare the GC–IMS fingerprints. Dynamic principal component analysis was performed using the “Dynamic PCA” plug-in that came with the instrument software. α-diversity analysis was conducted using the QIIME2 software, version 2019.4. Orthogonal partial least squares-discriminant analysis (OPLS-DA) and Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) were carried out using SIMCA 14.1 (Umetrics, Umea, Sweden).The Paisenuo cloud platform was used to apply linear discriminant analysis effect size and two-way orthogonal partial least squares, as well as to plot Sankey diagrams. Graphs depicting the relationships between dominant microbial communities and physicochemical properties, as well as between microorganisms and characteristic volatile compounds, were created using Spearman correlation coefficients.

## Results and analysis

### Physicochemical properties of yak yogurt

This study evaluated the physicochemical differences between yak yogurt fermented using commercial starter cultures (hereafter referred to as the CK group) and traditional starter cultures (hereafter referred to as the GN, QH, and XZ groups). The findings indicated that the traditional fermentation groups exhibited significantly higher total acidity, characteristic amino acid content, and short-chain fatty acid content compared with the CK group (P < 0.05), with the most pronounced differences observed in pH and total acidity levels. No significant differences were observed in total amino acid content among the traditional fermentation groups (P > 0.05). pH and total acidity are vital indicators for assessing the characteristics of yogurt fermentation. The XZ group had the highest total acidity (13.52 g/L) and the lowest pH (3.81), significantly lower than the other fermentation groups (P < 0.05). Conversely, the CK group had the highest pH (4.33) and the lowest total acidity (7.84 g/L). The pH values of the GN and XZ groups were significantly lower than those of the CK and QH groups, while their total acidity was significantly higher (P = 0.005), suggesting that starter cultures influence acid production during fermentation by modulating the proportion of acid-producing bacteria in the culture (Fig. 1A).

*Fig. 1: Comparative Analysis of Physicochemical Properties of Yak Yogurt Using Various Starter Cultures: (A) Variations in pH and total acidity of yak yogurt, (B) Heatmap illustrating amino acid profiles in yak yogurt, (C) Heatmap depicting fatty acid profiles in yak yogurt.*

Amino acids, which are protein degradation products, are crucial for the flavor profile of yak yogurt. The traditional fermentation groups showed significantly higher levels of characteristic amino acids (proline, arginine, alanine) compared with the CK group (P < 0.05). For example, proline (234.85 μg/g) and alanine (108.19 μg/g) contents in the XZ group were 2.8-fold and 2.1-fold higher than in the CK group, respectively. Additionally, the essential amino acid ratio in the XZ group significantly exceeded the standards recommended by the Food and Agriculture Organization/World Health Organization (ratio of essential-to-total amino acids = 68.98% and essential-to-non-essential amino acids = 88.63%).

Fatty acids modulate flavor characteristics by being converted into volatile compounds through oxidation and microbial metabolism. The CK group had a significantly higher long-chain fatty acid content (palmitic acid, stearic acid, oleic acid) than the traditional fermentation groups (P < 0.05), with palmitic acid levels being 8.4-fold higher than those in the GN group, potentially offering better industrial applicability. By contrast, the traditional fermentation groups contained significantly higher proportions of short-chain fatty acids, such as caproic acid (C6:0). Moreover, the distribution of specific fatty acids in the traditional fermentation groups varied by region. For example, behenic acid was detected in the QH group, while palmitoleic acid and myristoleic acid were absent in the GN and XZ groups, respectively, indicating metabolic selectivity differences among the microbial communities of different starter cultures (Fig. 1C).

### Analysis of volatile flavor compounds in yak yogurt

#### Qualitative assessment of volatile flavor compounds

A total of 59 volatile substances were identified across both commercial and traditional fermentation groups, comprising 46 known and 13 unknown compounds. Alcohols represented the largest category of volatile compounds identified, accounting for 27.12% of the total compounds, followed by esters (22.03%), ketones (15.26%), and aldehydes (8.47%; Fig. 2A). Significant differences (P < 0.05) were noted in the types and proportions of volatile flavor compounds between the commercial and traditional fermentation groups. The volatile flavor profile of the CK group was predominated by ketones, with a proportion of 62.66%, significantly surpassing the proportion of ketones in the traditional fermentation groups (Fig. 2B). The traditional fermentation groups displayed distinct regional characteristics. The XZ group had the highest alcohol content at 59.10%, while the QH group had a notably high ester content (36.74%). Although the ester content in the GN group was only 3.74%, the contents of aldehydes (such as isovaleraldehyde) and dimethyl sulfide were 31%–34% higher in the GN group compared with the QH and XZ groups (Fig. 2B).

*Fig. 2: Qualitative and Differential Analysis of Volatile Flavor Compounds in Yak Yogurt with Various Starter Cultures: (A) Qualitative analysis of volatile flavor compounds, (B) Relative content of volatile flavor compounds, (C) Three-dimensional HS-GC-IMS spectrum of volatile flavor compounds, (D) Differential HS-GC-IMS spectrum of volatile flavor compounds, (E) HS-GC-IMS fingerprint of volatile flavor compounds, (F) Radar plot illustrating volatile flavor compounds, (G) PCA score plot of volatile flavor compounds (H) Results of 200-time permutation tests for the PLS-DA model (R2 = 0.246, Q2 = − 0.682) .*

#### Comparative analysis of volatile compound profiles

A comparative study of volatile flavor compounds in yak yogurt fermented using commercial versus traditional starters was performed using headspace GC–IMS. Three-dimensional headspace GC–IMS spectra generated based on relative migration time, retention time, and signal peak intensity highlighted significant differences in volatile profiles between the commercial and traditional fermentation groups (Fig. 2C). The traditional fermentation groups exhibited a greater number and intensity of ion peaks, with the QH and XZ groups showing increased abundance and diversity of volatile flavor compounds. Differential spectra (Fig. 2D), derived by subtracting the volatile profile of the CK group, revealed more red dots in the 200–900 s range for the QH and XZ groups, indicating higher concentrations of volatile flavor compounds. Headspace GC–IMS fingerprint analysis corroborated the significant differences (P < 0.05) in volatile compound content between the commercial and traditional fermentation groups. The flavor compounds common to all the groups included acetoin monomer, acetoin dimer, and 2-propanone, all of which rendered creamy and fresh flavors to the yak yogurt (Fig. 2E–F). The CK group had the highest levels of unique flavor compounds, such as 2-butanone monomer, 2-pentanone, 2-propanol, and 2-heptanone monomer, which impart fruity notes (Fig. 2E–F). The GN group was rich in unique compounds such as 2-methyl-1-propanol monomer and dimer and 1-penten-3-ol. Methyl isovalerate and 1-penten-3-ol contributed fruity and floral aromas, while is valeraldehyde and isopropyl acetate contributed fresh herbal notes (Fig. 2E–F). The QH group had high concentrations of unique compounds such as ethyl acetate, 2-methyl-1-propyl acetate, and 2-methylpropanal. Ethyl acetate provided fruity notes while cyclohexanone provided a slightly pungent odor to the yogurt (Fig. 2E–F). The XZ group contained unique compounds such as 3-methylbutyl acetate monomer, ethanol, and 1-propanol dimer and polymer. Ethyl hexanoate and butanal added fruity aromas to the yogurt (Fig. 2E–F).

Cluster analysis of the principal component analysis plot revealed that PC1, PC2, and PC3 accounted for 46.50%, 29.20%, and 18.70% of the variance, respectively, with a cumulative contribution of 94.40%, effectively distinguishing samples from different starter cultures (Fig. 2G). The CK group samples were highly clustered and distinct from samples from the GN, QH, and XZ groups. The GN group was relatively close to the CK group, whereas the QH and XZ groups were further apart. The clear separation of the QH group from the CK group suggests high stability in the production of yak yogurt from the CK group, whereas the yogurt produced from traditional starter cultures displayed greater diversity and variation in volatile flavor compounds.

To objectively identify the key volatile compounds driving these observed differences, a supervised Orthogonal Projections to Latent Structures-Discriminant Analysis (OPLS-DA) was applied. The model's goodness-of-fit (R2Y(cum)) and predictive ability (Q2(cum), derived from 7-fold cross-validation) were 98.4% and 97.2%, respectively. To prevent model overfitting, a permutation test (200 iterations) was performed on the PLS-DA model, yielding intercepts of R2 = (0.0, 0.0893) and Q2 = (0.0, −0.819). These results confirm that the model exhibits good predictability and reproducibility without overfitting (Fig. S2A). Variable Importance in Projection (VIP) analysis of this validated model identified 14 compounds with VIP scores >1.0 as key discriminators, including 2-propanone, 2-pentanone, and ethyl acetate (Fig. S2B).The sensory relevance of these key markers was further validated by calculating their Odor Activity Values (OAV). Nine of the identified compounds, including 2-propanone, ethyl acetate and 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer, had OAV > 1, indicating a direct contribution to aroma. The remaining compounds (0.1 < OAV < 1) are considered important flavor modifiers (Table S2).

### Bacterial diversity in yak yogurt

#### Evaluation of bacterial diversity

Yak yogurt fermented using commercial starters exhibited a significantly different bacterial diversity profile compared with yogurt fermented using traditional starters (P < 0.05). The CK group displayed enhanced bacterial diversity and community evenness, as indicated by its higher Shannon index (P = 0.033), Simpson index (P = 0.027), and Pielou index (P = 0.019) compared with the traditional fermentation groups. Although the CK group showed the highest species richness based on the Chao1, abundance-based coverage estimator, and observed species indices, the variations in richness among the groups were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). The Good's coverage index was approaching 1, verifying that the sequencing depth for all samples was adequate and species coverage was comprehensive (Fig. 3A). The rarefaction curve indicated that the bacterial diversity of the CK group stabilized at approximately 150,000 sequences, while the traditional fermentation groups required greater sequencing depths, signifying that the CK group had higher species richness and diversity (Fig. 3B). Venn diagram analysis identified 95 shared amplicon sequence variants across all the groups, representing 3.1% of the total number of amplicon sequence variants. The XZ group featured the highest number of unique amplicon sequence variants (286), followed by the GN (233), QH (124), and CK (87) groups. These results emphasize the distinct bacterial profiles found in traditionally fermented yak yogurts (Fig. 3C). According to the principal component analysis plot, PC1 and PC2 accounted for 53.40% and 17.00% of the total variance, respectively, together contributing to 70.40% of the total variance. These components effectively differentiated yogurts on the basis of fermentation agents. The CK group formed a distinct and separate cluster, significantly distant from the three traditional fermentation groups, with the largest distance noted between the XZ and CK groups. The GN group appeared more dispersed, while the QH group was relatively concentrated (Fig. 3D).

#### Compositional analysis of bacterial communities

Metagenomic analysis provides insights into the taxonomic variations and region-specific characteristics of bacterial communities. In this study, metagenomic analysis uncovered significant differences (P < 0.05) between the bacterial communities found in yak yogurt fermented using commercial starters and traditional starters. At the phylum level, Firmicutes were predominant in the XZ group (96.08%) and least abundant in the CK group (55.48%), whereas Proteobacteria were most prevalent in the CK group (34.55%; Fig. 4A). At the class level, Bacilli dominated the XZ group (96.10%), while Gammaproteobacteria were most prominent in the CK group (32.93%; Fig. 4B). At the order level, Lactobacillales was the dominant order in the XZ group (95.88%), whereas Pseudomonadales were most prevalent in the CK group (25.71%; Fig. 4C). At the family level, Lactobacillaceae was the most prevalent family in the XZ group (88.34%), Pseudomonadaceae in the CK (24.79%) and GN (13.02%) groups, and Streptococcaceae in the QH (23.03%) and XZ groups (7.41%; Fig. 4D). At the genus level, Lactobacillus was the most abundant genus in the XZ (85.90%), GN (50.46%), QH (45.91%), and CK groups (44.30%), followed by Pseudomonas in the CK (24.15%) and GN groups (13.62%), and Streptococcus in the QH (22.76%) and XZ groups (7.51%; Fig. 4E). At the species level, L. delbrueckii was the dominant species in the XZ (49.56%) and GN groups (24.86%), followed by S. equinus in the CK group (18.30%) and S. thermophilus in the QH group (17.21%; Fig. 4F).

Linear discriminant analysis effect size further identified significant biomarkers in yak yogurt fermented using different starters, highlighting the regional adaptations in the bacterial communities of these starter cultures. Yak yogurts fermented using different starters contained distinctly different biomarkers (Fig. 4G). The CK group was enriched with L. amylovorus and L. fermentum, the GN group was enriched with L. delbrueckii subsp. bulgaricus and ethanol-tolerant Pediococcus, the QH group was enriched with L. thermophilus and L. fructivorans, and the XZ group was enriched with L. kefiri and cellulose-degrading bacterial communities.

### Interaction between physicochemical factors, flavor compounds, and bacterial communities in yak yogurt

Physicochemical factors and volatile flavor compounds share complex interactions in yak yogurt. Network heatmap analysis showed that a low pH was positively correlated with the abundance of acid-tolerant bacteria, such as L. delbrueckii, and negatively correlated with acid-sensitive bacteria, such as S. thermophilus. Glutamic acid, proline, and fatty acids can influence the bacterial community structure in both directions. Low pH (high acidity) was found to be positively correlated with the abundance of lactic acid bacteria, such as L. delbrueckii, L. amylovorus, and L. nasalidis (P < 0.01). This correlation was consistent with the known acid tolerance of these lactobacilli. Conversely, low pH was negatively correlated with the abundance of S. thermophilus and L. kefiranofaciens (P < 0.001). Glutamic acid content was positively correlated with the abundance of L. delbrueckii and L. nasalidis. Proline content was positively correlated with the abundance of L. amylovorus, L. equicursoris, and L. porci. However, proline content was negatively correlated with the abundance of S. thermophilus and L. kefiranofaciens. Arginine content was positively correlated with the abundance of L. delbrueckii and L. amylovorus (P < 0.01) and negatively correlated with the abundance of S. thermophilus and L. kefiranofaciens (P < 0.01). Fatty acids such as C18:1n9c, C16:0, and C14:0 were positively correlated with the abundance of L. amylovorus, L. equicursoris, and L. porci by enhancing the content of phosphatidylglycerol in bacterial cell membranes. However, these fatty acids were negatively correlated with the abundance of S. thermophilus and L. kefiranofaciens (P < 0.01; Fig. 5A).

Physicochemical factors also share complex interactions with volatile flavor compounds in yak yogurt. Heatmap analysis revealed that pH, total acidity, and amino acid content facilitated the accumulation of ketones and alcohols, as well as the generation of esters. Fatty acids boosted alcohol production but suppressed ester formation. pH was positively correlated with the levels of 2-propanone and 2-methyl-1-propanol dimer (P < 0.01), suggesting that alkaline conditions boost the accumulation of ketones and fusel alcohols. By contrast, pH was negatively correlated with 2-butanone dimer content (P ≤ 0.001), suggesting that acidic conditions keep unwanted ketone flavors in check. Total acidity was positively correlated with the levels of 2-propanone and 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer (P < 0.05), suggesting that ketone and alcohol pathways are activated in highly acidic conditions. However, total acidity was negatively correlated with the levels of 2-methyl-1-propyl acetate and acetic acid ethyl ester (P < 0.01), indicating that excessive acidity inhibits esterification. Glutamic acid content was positively correlated with 2-propanone levels (P < 0.001), driving acetone synthesis, and with 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer levels (P < 0.01), promoting fruity alcohol production. However, glutamic acid content was negatively correlated with the levels of 2-methyl-1-propanol dimer (r < −0.5), blocking the conversion of branched-chain α-keto acids to alcohols. Proline content was positively correlated with the levels of 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer and 2-methyl-1-propanol dimer (P < 0.001), serving as a precursor for higher alcohols. It was also positively correlated with 2-butanone dimer levels (P < 0.01), suggesting that the byproducts of proline decarboxylation lead to ketone formation. However, proline content was negatively correlated with the levels of 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer (P < 0.01), indicating that proline competitively inhibits ester synthesis. Arginine content was positively correlated with the levels of 2-propanone and alcohols (r > 0.5), suggesting that arginine supports alcohol/ketone synthesis as a nitrogen source. C18:1n9c content was positively correlated with the levels of 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer and 2-methyl-1-propanol dimer (r > 0.6), with C18:1n9c enhancing the accumulation of branched alcohols through the β-oxidation and Ehrlich pathways. However, C18:1n9c content was negatively correlated with ester content (r < −0.7, P ≤ 0.01), indicating that C18:1n9c inhibits esterase activity. The levels of C16:0 and C14:0 were positively correlated with the levels of alcohols and ketones (r > 0.5), suggesting that medium-chain fatty acids serve as ketone precursors and alcohol dehydrogenase cofactors. However, the levels of both were negatively correlated with ester content (r < −0.6), indicating that these medium-chain fatty acids disrupt the conformation of esterase and inhibit its activity (Fig. 5B). Overall, our results indicate that pH, total acidity, and amino acid content were positively associated with the accumulation of ketones and alcohols and the formation of esters, whereas fatty acids promoted alcohol production but hindered ester formation.

Bacterial communities and volatile flavor compounds also share complex interactions in yak yogurt. Network heatmap analysis revealed that L. delbrueckii is a key agent contributing to broad-spectrum esterification. S. thermophilus helps balance ketone and ester metabolism. Auxiliary bacteria modulate the flavor profile through substrate competition or synergistic synthesis. The abundance of L. delbrueckii was strongly positively correlated with the levels of esters such as 2-propanone, acetic acid ethyl ester, 3-methyl butyl acetate dimer, and 2-methyl-1-propyl acetate, highlighting the role of this bacterium in driving the synthesis of ethyl acetate and fruity esters. The abundance of S. thermophilus was positively correlated with the levels of 2-propanone and 2-butanone dimer, indicating its role in promoting ketone metabolism. It was also positively correlated with the levels of acetic acid ethyl ester and 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer, suggesting that this bacterium promotes esterification. However, S. thermophilus abundance was negatively correlated with 2-methyl-1-propanol dimer content, suppressing the off-flavors of fusel alcohols. The abundance of L. amylovorus, an auxiliary bacterium, was positively correlated with the levels of 2-propanone and 2-butanone dimer, suggesting that this bacterium contributes to ketone synthesis. Further, L. amylovorus abundance was negatively correlated with the levels of acetic acid ethyl ester and 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer, which is indicative of competitive inhibition of esterification pathways. The abundances of L. equicursoris and Mucilaginibacter glaciei were not correlated with 2-propanone levels but were positively correlated with the levels of acetic acid ethyl ester and 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer, confirming the roles of these bacteria in synergistic ester synthesis (Fig. 5C).

The spatial localization of bacterial communities and volatile flavor compounds was quantified using two-way orthogonal partial least squares analysis, and the loading plots revealed significant clustering between them (Fig. 5D). L. delbrueckii, L. kefiranofaciens, and S. thermophilus had high loading values, reflecting their strong contribution to principal components and their role in flavor formation. Among volatile compounds, acetic acid ethyl ester, 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer, and ketones such as 2-propanone and 2-heptanone monomer had high loading values, suggesting a strong link with bacterial communities. L. delbrueckii was spatially close to acetic acid ethyl ester and L. kefiranofaciens to 3-methylbutyl acetate dimer, indicating a positive correlation. This is consistent with the network heatmap results regarding the interactions between bacterial communities and volatile compounds in yak yogurt (Fig. 5C). The key contributors to flavor formation were identified through two-way orthogonal partial least squares importance ranking plots, which highlighted the prominent strains driving volatile compound synthesis. The top bacterium was L. delbrueckii, followed by S. thermophilus. Among the volatile compounds, 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer was the most important, followed by acetic acid ethyl ester and 2-propanone (Fig. 5E; Fig. S1).

### Role of lactic acid bacteria in the formation of flavor compounds

Using the PICRUSt2 software and KEGG metabolic pathway analysis, we further elucidated the contributions of Lactobacillus spp. and Streptococcus spp. to the flavor profiles of yak yogurts fermented with different starters. Beta diversity analysis showed that these yogurts share core metabolic pathways, such as carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism. However, lipid and energy metabolism was more enriched in the XZ group, suggesting that different starters affect bacterial metabolic functions differently (Fig. 6A). A Sankey diagram was created, illustrating how L. delbrueckii and S. thermophilus generate important flavor compounds through various KEGG pathways. In both strains, the synthesis of 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer involved ATP-binding cassette transporters (ko02010) and branched-chain amino acid degradation (ko00280), with quorum sensing pathways (ko02024) also playing a role in L. delbrueckii. The synthesis of acetic acid ethyl ester involved a greater diversity of pathways, with both strains employing glycolysis (ko00010), pyruvate metabolism (ko00620), fatty acid degradation (ko00071), and the phosphotransferase system (ko02060) for precursor supply and reaction catalysis. L. delbrueckii was also found to provide energy via oxidative phosphorylation (ko00190) and secrete enzymes through the bacterial secretion system (ko03070) to aid esterification. For 2-propanone synthesis, L. delbrueckii was found to use the AMP-associated protein kinase signaling pathway (ko04152), glycolysis (ko00010), and pyruvate metabolism (ko00620), whereas S. thermophilus was found to use oxidative phosphorylation (ko00190). The shared fatty acid degradation pathway (ko00071) was also crucial for 2-propanone production (Fig. 6B; Fig. S1).

## Discussion

Yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters exhibited distinct profiles in total acidity, characteristic amino acids, and diversity of short-chain fatty acids compared to that fermented with commercial starters. The observed differences are associated with three major areas of metabolic variation supported by the data. First, the variation in total acidity correlates with differing organic acid synthesis pathways. Traditional starters, including L. plantarum, produce both lactic and acetic acids via the phosphoketolase pathway. The interaction between S. thermophilus and L. casei were associated with pyruvate dehydrogenase, leading to butyric acid accumulation and increased total organic acid content (Lang, Wen, Wu, Pan and Wang, 2022a, Lang, Wen, Wu, Pan and Wang, 2022b; Paszczyk & Tońska, 2022). By contrast, commercial starters rely on a single β-galactosidase pathway, causing an imbalance in lactic and acetic acid production and insufficient acidity (Matela et al., 2019). Second, the differences in characteristic amino acids correlate with variations in proteolytic activity. Yak yogurt contains 34% more β-lactoglobulin than regular cow yogurt, offering a unique substrate for traditional starters. The high activity of extracellular peptidases in traditional starters was positively correlated with amino acid accumulation and intracellular pH homeostasis during acidification (Ulmer et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2021). The cell wall proteinase PrtP cleaves κ-casein to release proline, and the intracellular peptidase system (PepX/PepN) breaks down oligopeptides into flavor amino acids such as alanine (Rodríguez-Serrano et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2024a, Yu et al., 2024b). In commercial starters, however, the LacS transporter is overactivated, leading to the synthesis of non-essential amino acids such as glutamic acid, which disrupts the balance between essential and non-essential amino acids (Hashemi et al., 2017). Third, the diversity in short-chain fatty acids correlated with distinct lipid metabolism. In commercial starters, high Lp_3563 lipase activity was positively correlated with long-chain fatty acid enrichment. By contrast, in traditional microbial starters such as L. plantarum A3, the cold-shock protein CspA was upregulated, boosting esterase activity and favoring the synthesis of short-chain fatty acids, such as capric acid (Khademi et al., 2022). This process reduces lipid peroxidation and retains functional lipids such as myristoleic acid. These findings are in alignment with previous findings (Lang et al., 2022).

The profiles of volatile flavor compounds in yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters differ significantly from those in yogurt fermented with commercial starters owing to differences in microbial metabolic synergy. First, regional bacterial communities and raw material characteristics in traditional fermentation were associated with a complex and diverse flavor profile. Commercial starters, designed for uniformity, show a strong positive correlation with ketone synthesis via standardized strains (Yang et al., 2023). Second, bacterial symbiosis and adaptation to challenging conditions are responsible for the flavor complexity associated with traditional fermentation. For instance, in the XZ group, alcohol dehydrogenase was positively correlated with low temperatures to produce ethyl hexanoate; in the QH group, ethyl acetate was associated with the phosphoketolase pathway; in the GN group, Pseudomonas spp. converts linoleic acid into aldehydes in a cold, humid environment. Lactobacillus spp. stabilize aldehydes by synthesizing citrulline through the arginine deiminase pathway, consistent with previous studies (Bintsis & Papademas, 2022; Zhao et al., 2024). Third, the interaction between bacterial metabolic networks were associated with regional flavor profile of yak yogurt. Ketone enrichment in the CK group was strongly correlated with the targeted metabolism of standardized strains (Vénica et al., 2023). By contrast, traditional fermentation groups have varied flavor compositions were correlated with regional diversity. For example, the predominance of alcohols in the XZ group is a result of lactic acid bacteria regenerating coenzymes to form propanol polymers. The abundance of esters in the QH group is a consequence of the interaction between the esterase activity of lactic acid bacteria and short-chain fatty acid substrates. The enrichment of aldehydes and sulfur compounds in the GN group can be attributed to branched-chain amino acid deamination and sulfur metabolism (Liu et al., 2022). In summary, traditional starters were associated with the activate diverse metabolic pathways through microbial synergy and natural selection, whereas the single microbial community in commercial starters was correlated with a more uniform metabolite profile.

Traditional starters exhibit more bacterial diversity than commercial starters. This higher diversity was correlated with regional environmental factors, microbial interactions, and metabolic synergy. First, the traditional fermentation groups in this study (GN, QH, XZ) displayed high Lactobacillus diversity and regional strain enrichment. They create region-specific microbial networks through interactions. By contrast, the CK group maintain microbial uniformity but loses diversity, as demonstrated in previous studies (Huang et al., 2023; Obioha et al., 2021). Second, traditional fermentation groups have more unique species than the CK group, which is a manifestation of the competitive exclusion effect of commercial starters. The high-altitude environment of Tibet favors Firmicutes (96.08%) and L. delbrueckii (49.56%), which enhance cold metabolism through the cspA gene, thus maintaining intracellular pH stability, which is crucial for maintaining high acidity in the XZ group (Peng et al., 2021). The temperature variations in Qinghai was correlated with S. thermophilus, which is efficient in whey proteins to produce esters via β-galactosidase (Li, Yang, Shi, et al., 2024). The grazing environment of Gannan was associated with Pseudomonas spp., which synthesize aldehydes through the lipoxygenase pathway (Zinno et al., 2022). Third, in the XZ and QH groups, Lactobacillus spp. and Streptococcus spp. exhibit a dynamic balance through bacteriocin inhibition and biofilm competition, and this balance is regulated by raw materials rich in fat (promoting membrane lipid synthesis in Lactobacillus spp.) and lactose (promoting glycolysis in Streptococcus spp.) (Brodziak et al., 2021). Commercial starters profiles were characterized by ketone flavor, which is consistent with previous findings (Zhang et al., 2025). Geographically, the XZ and QH groups reflect the convergent evolution of Lactobacillus spp. due to cold plateau environments, while the GN and QH groups reflect the metabolic differences between Pseudomonas and Streptococcus spp. due to rainfall differences (Bai et al., 2024). These associations provide biomarkers for origin tracing, such as the kefir Lactobacillus gene marker in the XZ group (Ding et al., 2022; Peng et al., 2021). Lactobacillus spp. and related bacterial groups drive fermentation. Starter culture type and regional conditions were key factors correlating with final microbial community structure and metabolism.

Interactions among regional characteristics, microbes, and metabolites were correlated with flavor complexity in traditional yak yogurt. Lactic acid bacteria play a key role in this process. L. delbrueckii produces ethyl acetate by converting glucose to pyruvate through glycolysis and glycerolipid metabolism. In acidic conditions, the esterase activity increases, and the esterification efficiency is boosted (Moonga et al., 2021; Shah et al., 2023). Glutamate availability was associated with branched-chain amino acids in Lactobacillus kefiranofaciens, leading to the production of 3-methylbutyl acetate, which confers a fruity aroma (Brodziak et al., 2021). Fatty acids help inhibit the infusion of off-flavors. S. thermophilus suppresses acetone production by blocking fatty acid β-oxidation (ko00071), and this effect can be mitigated by C16:0. L. delbrueckii uses quorum sensing (ko02024) to regulate the ilvE/kivD gene cluster, improving the conversion efficiency of branched-chain amino acids. It also secretes esterases (ko03070) to promote esterification (Rodríguez-Serrano et al., 2018). S. thermophilus maintains energy levels by boosting sugar transport via the phosphotransferase system (ko02060) and oxidative phosphorylation (ko00190). Both strains are synchronized in their metabolic functions through ATP-binding cassette transporters (ko02010), glycolysis (ko00010), fatty acid degradation (ko00071), AMP-associated protein kinase signaling (ko04152), and secretion systems (ko03070) (Zhong et al., 2025).Traditional fermentation groups favor acid-tolerant microbes such as L. delbrueckii, which dominate and shape the community. Amino acids guide bacteria were correlated with specific flavors, and fatty acids control the intensity of flavor inhibition (Matela et al., 2019). Commercial groups, which are lacking in microbial diversity, exhibited a more limited metabolism of flavor compounds (Dan et al., 2019; Uttarwar et al., 2024; Yanting et al., 2025). In summary, the aforementioned pathways contribute to the distinct flavor of yak yogurt from the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau (Li et al., 2024; Yu et al., 2024).

The CK group serves as the gold standard for industrial yak yogurt production. It showed high stability, with highly concentrated clustering of flavor compounds in the principal component analysis plot. Moreover, it displayed microbial uniformity, with a significantly higher Shannon index compared with traditional groups. This ensures controlled fermentation (pH = 4.33, acidity 7.84 g/L) but also reveals three major metabolic deficiencies. From the aspect of nutrition, the presence of Pseudomonadales at a proportion of 25.71% was associated with abnormal accumulation of long-chain fatty acids, with the content of palmitic acid being 8.4-fold higher than that in the GN group. This results in essential amino acid ratios not meeting the standards set by the Food and Agriculture Organization, reflected in the proline content, which was only 35.70% of the proline content in the traditional groups. From the aspect of flavor, a significant negative correlation between C16:0/C18:1n9c content and ester content implies that the activity of esterase is inhibited, resulting in ketones accounting for 62.66% of the total flavor compounds and a severe deficiency of esters. From the functional aspect, microbial diversity does not translate into metabolic advantages because the microbial community is dominated by starch-degrading Lactobacillus and fermenting Lactobacillus. This in sharp contrast with the traditional groups, wherein L. delbrueckii efficiently converts fatty acids into esters after alcohol formation. Overall, the three metabolic deficiencies exposed by commercial starters reveal the core finding of this study—in the unique microecological environment of yak yogurt, the competitive/symbiotic interactions between standardized commercial starters and native yogurt microbiota ultimately lead to indigenous lactic acid bacteria dominating the microbial community structure in the final product. This adaptive deficiency mechanism highlights the ecological niche advantage of traditional starters. On the basis of the advantages of traditional starters in key metabolic mechanisms and quality characteristics, targeted improvements were made to the quality defects in the CK group by transplanting functional strains from traditional fermentation groups. Nutritional improvement was achieved by co-culturing with L. kefir from the XZ group and overexpressing proline iminopeptidase, which activated quorum sensing cross-regulation (ko02024) to increase the proportion of essential amino acids to 65.00%. Flavor optimization involved introducing the L. delbrueckii ester synthase gene (atf1) from the QH group, adding 0.1% sodium butyrate precursor, and incorporating the S. thermophilus phosphotransferase sugar transport system (ko02060). These changes helped increase the ester proportion from 22.03% to 30.00%. Post-acidification control was achieved by integrating the arginine deiminase pathway from ethanol-tolerant Pediococcus of the GN group and combining it with a 0.1% citrate buffer system, which maintained the final storage acidity ≤85°T. In summary, through the technical paradigm of functional module disassembly of traditional strains and targeted enhancement of commercial starters, a dual-stability process of acidity and flavor was developed with stage temperature control and precursor addition, ultimately creating a new paradigm for the CK group that combines traditional flavor with industrial advantages.

## Conclusion

This study highlights the superior physicochemical properties and complex flavor profiles of yak yogurt fermented with traditional starters from the Qinghai–Tibet Plateau compared to commercial starters. Key findings include increased acidity and enriched amino acid and short-chain fatty acid contents, which contribute to unique regional flavors characterized by higher concentrations of esters and alcohols. The functional specialization and coordination of L. delbrueckii and S. thermophilus directs a network of pathways, including glycolysis and ABC transport, to produce defining volatile compounds including 3-methylbutan-1-ol dimer, ethyl acetate, and 2-pentanone. This underscores the importance of interactions between microbial communities and metabolites in flavor formation and provides a rational roadmap for flavor-targeted design in fermented yak yogurt production. Future studies must leverage integrated multi-omics across broader geographical samples to delineate the core microbial and metabolic drivers of yak yogurt quality and the strain-specific pathways linking microbiota to distinct flavor compounds, thereby enabling the rational design of specialized fermentation agents for standardized production.
